newsitem.title: USA: U.S. military's anti-terrorism measures faulted.
newsitem.headline: U.S. military's anti-terrorism measures faulted.

text.p: A congressional report said on Monday that one year after a deadly bomb attack in Saudi Arabia the U.S. Defence Department had failed to put in place a comprehensive system to protect U.S. forces against terrorist attacks.

The General Accounting Office, the investigative arm of Congress, said it had sent teams in March and April this year to 30 overseas military sites to inspect measures in place to protect U.S. forces against terrorist attacks.
"We found significant security improvements have been made in Turkey and the Middle East to protect against vehicle bombs," it said but added "vulnerabilities remain."
In particular, it said recommendations in a report prepared by retired Army Gen. Wayne Downing for more common standards and more consistent "vulnerability assessments" were not being implemented.
"Vulnerability assessments lack consistency because DOD (the Department of Defence) has not established common standards for them," the GAO report said.
It said more guidance was needed to commanders around the world to help them establish whether they have put enough anti-terrorist measures in place.
It said worldwide standards should be developed for "stand-off" distance -- the distance military facilities should be from roads or public places to prevent attacks by, for example, truck bombs.
The Downing report was triggered by the June, 1996 truck bombing of the Khobar Towers housing facility near Dharhan in Saudi Arabia that killed 19 American servicemen.

The GAO noted that the Pentagon had responded to a major recommendation of the Downing report and established a special department under the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff for combating terrorism.
It also said that it found evidence that commanders "at all levels were placing more emphasis on the anti-terrorism programme than they had prior to Khobar Towers."

But it concluded that "In our view, DOD's failure to impose a comprehensive approach to combating terrorism, as envisioned by the Downing task force, has resulted in a programme that still lacks consistency and coordination."

It also said although extra precautions had been put in place areas of high risk like the Middle East, the Pentagon had "placed less emphasis on improving security at sites where the terrorist threat is not considered to be high."
